policy.records: Only the reads that differ from what LibreOffice made of the same file, and only the renders that do not land in the clean band. Everything this suite exercises that is absent from the two lists below is asserted to agree, so a new difference fails by not being listed.
policy.reproduce: A row that stops reproducing fails too. That is deliberate: a fix should arrive with this file updated, so the shrinking of the suspected-defect list is a thing somebody can point at. A render that comes back better than the band recorded here fails for the same reason - an improvement nobody records is an improvement nobody can show.
policy.states: documented - a limitation one of the conformance documents states. suspected-defect - a difference nobody decided on, which is what comparing against another implementation is actually good for. accepted - this component's own behaviour, looked at and accepted.
policy.reviewer: A row is not classified by being written down. documented and accepted both need a reviewer and a date, and a documented row needs a reference to the conformance document that states the limitation, which the guard checks is really there. This is the same demand CorpusControlGuardTests makes of the corpus baseline and PdfTestControlGuardTests makes of the tool manifest.
policy.toolchain: producedWith pins the LibreOffice build, the PDF text extractor, the font set, the platform and the dpi these rows were measured on. A run whose own stamp does not match it does not compare against these rows: it skips, and the skip names the mismatch. LibreOffice's layout moves between releases and with whatever fonts it can find, so a row measured on another machine is a claim about that machine, and quietly reading it as a claim about this one is how a suite comes to fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the change under test.
policy.empty: Both lists ship empty and every producedWith field is null, because nothing has been measured here against an approved, pinned toolchain yet. That is the shipped state on purpose, and it is not the same as having no opinion. An empty file says plainly that nothing has been measured; a file generated against whatever LibreOffice happened to be installed that morning looks like evidence, and would be worse than no baseline for exactly that reason. tests/corpus/external-sources.json ships with no rows on the same argument.
policy.bands: A render row records bands, not numbers. The numbers under observed are there for a reader, and for hysteresis when a run sits on a threshold; the verdict is the band. Rasterized comparison numbers move with antialiasing, hinting and the version of the font that got installed, so a file that recorded them as the expectation would fail on a change nobody can see and pass on one anybody could.

reads.why: Not a difference at all - the text projections agree, and the row exists only because the read raised html.css.rule. That is the codec reporting that it skipped a stylesheet rule whose selector it does not implement, which here is the 'td p' and 'th p' that LibreOffice writes for a table. Reporting it is the behaviour this component asks of a codec, so the row records a codec doing the right thing loudly. docs/notes/html.md states exactly which selector is matched and which are not, and why the line is drawn there.
reads.reviewer: Claude Opus 5, on the first office baseline

reads.why: Not a difference this component could avoid. LibreOffice's HTML export has no way to write a frame, so it flattens both of the seed's frames to GIF files beside the document and links them; the reader never fetches an external resource and reports html.skip.external once per read, which docs/notes/html.md states outright in both directions. What the row is worth recording for is what it says about the corpus rather than about the codec: the html target of this seed measures a document with the construct taken out of it, so a reader comparing the four targets knows not to read agreement here as evidence about frames.
reads.reviewer: Claude Opus 5, on the letterhead and line-break seeds

reads.why: A limitation docs/notes/html.md states outright: the HTML writer does not emit list structure and reports html.list when it drops it, so a list read from HTML does not survive a round trip back through HTML. The roadmap holds HTML list writing as deliberate and unimplemented, to be reconsidered only behind conformance fixtures and explicit diagnostics. The diagnostic is the codec saying what it dropped, which is the half that makes the limitation reviewable.

reads.why: The same kind of difference, in the other place docs/guides/cli.md names. LibreOffice's text export joins a table row onto one line - 'cell a cell b' - and this component's gives each cell its own line, in row order, because that is how the model holds a table once it is flattened and a joined row would invent a column separator the document never stated. Neither reader lost a cell.

renders.why: LibreOffice cannot write a frame into HTML, so it flattens both of this seed's frames to GIF files beside the document; the reader never fetches an external resource and says so with html.skip.external, which docs/notes/html.md states in both directions. The <div title="header"> container is now recognized and extracted into RunningContent rather than leaking into body content. What remains is the skipped external frame GIFs and absent @page geometry in LibreOffice's HTML export.
renders.reviewer: Claude Opus 5, on the letterhead and line-break seeds

renders.why: A disagreement rather than a defect, and the one place in this corpus where following the format costs a band. \titlepg is read now, so this component draws no footer on the first page of a section that states one and names no \footerf - which is what Word does. LibreOffice draws the default footer there, and the 1193 px is the whole of the difference: it inks the bottom of page one and this component inks nothing below the third line. Matching LibreOffice would have been the cheaper number and the worse answer, because its own DOCX importer honours the same flag the Word way - agreeing with it here would have made this component disagree with itself across two of its own readers. The stray page number the text and interop rows recorded is gone: a field result belongs to the destination the field is in. What the profile still reads is the gradient, which runs left to right here where ODT and DOCX now run it down the page - LibreOffice writes no fillAngle into its RTF at all and renders its own file bottom-to-top, so no reading of that document agrees with all three of the source, the oracle and the other two targets.
renders.reviewer: Claude Opus 5, on the reader fixes the letterhead seed found
